TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF:
LD 1515 "An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use
Tax"
THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON TAXATION

Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and distinguished members of the
Taxation Committee. I am Representative Amy Arata, and it is my honor to represent House District 104, which includes New Gloucester and part of Gray. . It's my pleasure to introduce LD 1515 "An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted
Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax."
The idea for this bill came from one of my constituents, who asked me why
wheelchair adapted vehicles are exempt from sales tax in other states, but not in Maine. The adaptive equipment which is installed in vehicles to make them operable by a person with a disability is sales tax exempt. However, in order for a person to be able to get a wheelchair into a vehicle, the vehicle itself must be modified, such as by lowering the floor. Also, it must be a larger vehicle than
average, such as a van or truck, and therefore more expensive. A small used
Camry isn't an option for most people in wheelchairs, so wheelchair users must purchase a more expensive vehicle than they otherwise would.
Many states exempt wheelchair adapted vehicles from sales and use tax. They
include Alabama, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan,
Mississippi, New Jersey, New Mexico, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, West
Virginia, and others. Several states offer sales tax or excise tax exemptions for
100% disabled veterans. In order to prove that one qualifies for the exemption,
states often require a signed affidavit stating that the vehicle will be used by a
disabled person. A similar requirement may be appropriate for Maine.

Proudly Serving House District 104
New Gloucester/ Gray (Part)

As l prepared this bill, l consulted with MobilityWorks, a nationwide provider of
wheelchair vans which has a dealership in Gray. They told me that it currently
takes about four months to have a vehicle modified to work with adaptive
equipment. For this reason, I included a provision that allows the modification to occur within six months of purchase.
In Maine, we exempt manytthings that are necessities of life, such as food,
prescribed medicine, heating fuel, and even automobiles used in driver education
programs. Wheelchair adapted vehicles are a necessity of life in order for many people to lead full and productive lives, such as Marcel Hug and Susannah Scaroni, who won the Boston Marathon on Monday. You'll hear testimonies in support of
this bill from business owners, political candidates, and foster parents and family
members who care for people with special needs. Their lives aren't easy, but by passing this bill the legislature can show that we are willing to help where we have
the power to do so. Thank you for your consideration and l'm happy to answer
any questions.
Respectfully,

Brian Harnish Orono LD 1515
April 23, 2025 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333
In Support of LD 1515 - An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax
Good Afternoon, Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee,
My name is Brian, and I am submitting this written testimony in support of LD 1515, "An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax."
I've had my driver's license for 15 years, and I use hand controls to drive due to my disability. I live in an urban part of Maine where some resources are available, but even here, the process of becoming a driver and maintaining an adapted vehicle is expensive and complicated. I had to pay $500 just for an assessment to figure out what kind of adaptive equipment I needed--and that was before any modifications were actually made.
The hand controls I use now are a very basic setup, and they still cost over $1,000 out of pocket. Vehicle modification shops often charge over $100 per hour for labor. These costs add up fast, and for many people with disabilities--especially those living on fixed incomes--this can be a huge barrier to independence.
I'd also like to urge you to consider people with disabilities who live in rural areas of Maine. In places where public transportation is not an option, owning an adapted vehicle is often the only way to get to work, medical appointments, the grocery store, or community events. For many, it's the difference between being part of their community or being isolated.
LD 1515 would help offset the overwhelming costs associated with purchasing and modifying a vehicle for wheelchair access. Removing the sales tax is a small step that can have a big impact--giving more people the chance to live and travel independently.
This bill is about more than money. It's about mobility, dignity, and equal opportunity. I strongly urge you to support LD 1515.
Thank you for your time and for considering the real, everyday needs of Mainers with disabilities.
Sincerely, Brian Harnish Orono, ME

Testimony of Hon. Dale Crafts
IN SUPPORT of LD 1515 " An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and use tax
Senator Grohosski, Representative Cloutier, and honorable members of the joint standing committee on taxation
My name is Dale Crafts; it's an honor to be here before your committee. Thank you for serving the Maine people. It truly is a sacrifice to serve. Back in May of 1983 I was traveling to work on my motorcycle when an elderly man turned in front of me, forcing me off the road. When I woke from the accident, I realized I couldn't move my body from the chest down. So, the journey began as a paraplegic. Next month will be 42 years in a chair. I would like to show you one example of how expensive medical equipment cost. This manual Wheelchair cost with the cushion is $8200. Now I will talk to you what it is like to purchase a wheelchair adaptable vehicle. 2018 I bought leftover 2017 GMC 4 door Siera truck and had it converted. The cost of the conversion in 2018 was $30,000. That conversion today cost $ 39.000. Not counting the cost of the truck. The cost of the same truck and conversion today would be over $100,000. The van I drive now is a Chrysler Pacifica converted by BraunAbility that I purchased from MobilityWorks in Gray Maine. I I'm the second owner of this van, the first owner bought new at cost of $98,000. I purchased this same van as second owner April 19, 2023, for the amount of $73,044. with monthly payment amount of $1,134. for 60 months. I believe very few disable person could afford that high of a payment without help from family or other sources. I would like to tell you how important it is to get your independence back by having the ability to get in a vehicle and drive off on your own. It's game changes psychologically and mentally. Over the year I had have several families ask me to please talk to a person that has become paralyzed to show them that life isn't over. One of the first thing I tell them, if possible, get yourself a handicap adapted transportation as soon as possible. Its life changing. I encourage list committee to pass LD1515 with a unanimous vote and pray that appropriation will fund it. God bless each and every one of you. Thank you for your time. Is there any questions?

David Lawrence Portland LD 1515
April 22, 2025 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333 Testimony in Support of LD 1515 - An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax Senator Grohoski, Representative Perry, and Members of the Committee on Taxation, My name is David, and I live in Portland. I'm writing today to express my support for LD 1515, a bill to exempt wheelchair-adapted vehicles from the sales and use tax. This bill is important to me because I have a disability and drive a modified vehicle. While I am not currently in a wheelchair, I know people who are, and I understand how essential accessible vehicles are to independence and mobility. Whether you're in a wheelchair or need hand controls, modified vehicles come with very high costs beyond the price of the car itself. For example, my current vehicle has a left-foot accelerator and a steering knob to help me drive. That setup alone added about $1,800 to the cost of my car. It's a big expense, and I know others pay even more--especially when full wheelchair access or lifts are needed. Many people with disabilities rely on fixed incomes like Social Security or SSDI. It doesn't make sense to charge sales tax on something that is not a luxury, but a necessity. Taking away the sales tax on these kinds of vehicles would help people afford safe, appropriate transportation and stretch their limited income further. It's not just about getting around--it's about staying independent, getting to work, visiting friends, and participating in the community. I would also like to suggest that this bill be expanded in the future to include all modified vehicles--not just ones adapted for wheelchair access. There are many of us with different physical needs who require other types of adaptive equipment to drive safely. If we're investing in accessibility, we should recognize all types of vehicle modifications that support people with disabilities. This bill is a step in the right direction toward making life more affordable and accessible. I hope you will support LD 1515 and consider how we can keep building on it to help more Mainers live independently. Thank you for your time and for considering my testimony. Sincerely, David Lawrence, SUFU Member Portland, Maine

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: April 23, 2025, Wednesday at 1:00 P.M.
LD 1515 - "An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Neither For Nor Against LD 1515, "An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax."
This bill would exempt from sales and use tax the sale of an automobile if it is either adapted for use by an occupant in a wheelchair, or if the purchaser attests it will be so adapted within 6 months of purchase. If the Committee supports this bill, we strongly recommend amending the proposed exemption as a refund provision in the cases of a customer attesting that the vehicle will be modified post-purchase.
The Sales and Use Tax Law currently exempts "sales to a person with a disability . . . of adaptive equipment for installation in or on a motor vehicle to make that vehicle operable or accessible by a person with a disability who is issued a disability plate or placard . . . ." 36 M.R.S. � 1760(95). This applies only to the adaptive equipment, not the vehicle in which it is installed. Likewise, the Governor's Biennial Budget, Part G, proposes a related sales tax exemption for "mobility enhancing equipment" for home use or use in a motor vehicle; but would define "mobility enhancing equipment" to exclude "any motor vehicle or
1

equipment on a motor vehicle normally provided by a motor vehicle manufacturer."
LD 1515 would allow customers to purchase any "automobile" exempt of sales tax if they "attest [wheelchair] modifications are necessary and will be completed within 6 months of the vehicle's purchase." This suggests each purchaser claiming the exemption on an unmodified automobile would be required to present an affidavit to the retailer to purchase the automobile without paying tax. Rather than an up-front exemption from sales tax for automobiles intended to be modified to accommodate wheelchairs, this part of the proposal would be better administered as a refund, where the refund is requested from MRS upon completion of the automobile's modifications.
"Automobile" as defined in the Sales and Use Tax Law means "a selfpropelled 4-wheel motor vehicle designed primarily to carry passengers and not designed to run on tracks," and includes a pickup truck or van with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 pounds or less. As drafted, the exemption would not extend to a motor vehicle that is not an "automobile." The committee may also consider including language similar to that in � 1760(95), requiring that the purchaser has been "issued a disability plate or placard by the Secretary of State pursuant to Title 29A, section 521."
The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill; representatives from MRS will be here for the Work Session to provide additional information and respond in detail to the Committee's questions.

Regina Bowie Presque Isle LD 1515
April 23, 2025 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333 Testimony in Support of LD 1515 - An Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax Senator Grohoski, Representative Perry, and Members of the Committee on Taxation, My name is Regina, and I'm speaking today in support of LD 1515, which would remove the sales and use tax on wheelchair-adapted vehicles. I believe this bill is really important because people who use wheelchairs already face higher costs when it comes to transportation and mobility. Vehicles that are adapted for wheelchair users or people with physical disabilities can be extremely expensive, and that includes the modifications--things like hand controls, ramps, and specialized equipment. These aren't luxuries--they're necessities for people who want to live their lives and get around safely. It's not just about getting in and out of the vehicle--it's also about being able to operate it safely. People need adaptive equipment that includes things like hand controls and good brake control, especially for those who may not have full use of their legs. This is critical for safe driving. In some cases, visual or auditory supports are also needed to help the person operate the vehicle confidently and independently. I also believe this exemption should apply to both drivers and passengers. Some people, like my friend Kevin, need to remain in their wheelchair while riding in the vehicle, even though they don't drive. Others might have partial paralysis and are still able to drive, but only with special equipment to help them do it safely and comfortably. These vehicles and modifications are expensive. Removing the sales tax would make a big difference in helping people afford what they need. It would help more people with disabilities get access to transportation, be more independent, and connect with their communities--just like everyone else. I truly hope you support this bill and help make life more accessible and safe for Mainers with disabilities. Thank you. Sincerely, Regina Bowie Presque Isle, ME crystalunicorn73@spectrum.net

May 7, 2025
Senator Nicole Grohoski Representative Kristen Cloutier Joint Standing Committee on Taxation State House, Room 127 Augusta, ME 04335
LD 1515, Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax
Dear Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation;
My name is Sara Squires and I am the Public Policy Director at Disability Rights Maine (DRM), Maine's designated Protection and Advocacy (P&A) agency for people with disabilities. On behalf of DRM and the individuals we serve, I am submitting this testimony in support of LD 1515, Act to Exempt Wheelchair Adapted Vehicles from the Sales and Use Tax.
It is no secret that transportation is a challenge here in Maine. From the lack of a robust public transit system to ongoing concerns about Maine's Non-Emergency Transportation program and the rising costs of motor vehicles, individuals across the state face significant barriers to accessing reliable and accessible transportation. This issue disproportionately affects individuals with disabilities.
For individuals for individuals with disabilities who require modified vehicles to accommodate wheelchairs or other assistive mobility devices, the cost of obtaining a suitable vehicle is often much higher than for those without such needs. As noted in the testimony of others, wheelchair-adapted vehicles--whether vans, minivans, or sport utility vehicles--are not purchased out of preference, but out of necessity. Smaller vehicles simply do not meet their needs.
160 Capitol Street, Suite 4, Augusta, ME 04330 207.626.2774 � 1.800.452.1948 � Fax: 207.621.1419 � drme.org
MAINE'S PROTECTION AND ADVOCACY AGENCY FOR PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES

This is not a theoretical issue. It is one I personally experienced. In November 2023, the transmission failed on my vehicle. It had been my first vehicle, and I had it for 19 years. The process of obtaining a new vehicle was long and challenging, especially given the specific accommodations I required. As a scooter user, I needed a list that would fit into the new vehicle, and I knew I would need a larger vehicle to ensure this was possible. While I ultimately found a vehicle that met my needs, the cost of purchasing it--including $2,100 in sales tax--was significant and added a financial burden to an already stressful situation. The additional financial burden of purchasing either an adapted vehicle or a vehicle that can be modified often prevents individuals with disabilities from acquiring the transportation they need. Whether through an exemption from the sales tax or, as the Maine Revenue Service suggests, a refund after purchase, DRM strongly supports any effort to reduce financial barriers and make adaptive vehicles more affordable for those who need them. Accessible transportation is vital for individuals with disabilities to maintain their independence, participate in the workforce, and access the services they need. I urge you to support LD 1515 and help make it easier for Mainers with disabilities to obtain the adapted vehicles they rely on. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely,
Sara Squires Public Policy Director Disability Rights Maine
